title: Notations
body_md: We use standard asymptotic notation. For two sequences $a_n,b_n$, we write $a_n\ll b_n$ if $a_n/b_n\to0$; $a_n\gg b_n$ if $b_n/a_n\to0$; and $a_n\sim b_n$ if $a_n/b_n\to1$. We additionally write $b_n = o(a_n)$ to denote any sequence $b_n\ll a_n$; $\omega(a_n)$ to denote any sequence $b_n\gg a_n$; $b_n=\mathcal{O}(a_n)$ if $\lim\sup_{n\to\infty}|b_n/a_n|<\infty$; $b_n=\Omega(a_n)$ if $\lim\inf_{n\to\infty}|b_n/a_n|>0$; and $b_n=\Theta(a_n)$ if $a_n=\mathcal{O}(b_n)$ and $b_n=\mathcal{O}(a_n)$.

label: thm:estimation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:estimation}
Suppose that the graph is generated according to $G(n,p_n,\alpha,\xi)$, with $1 \ll np_n \ll n^{2\alpha-1} / \log n $, $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$, and $\xi\in(0,1]$. 
Then, there exist estimators $\hat{K}_1$, $\hat{K}_2$, $\hat{\alpha}$, $\hat{p}$ and $\hat{\xi}$, computed from the exploration times $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{time}}$ of a single continuous-time FPP process with known rate $\lambda=1$, such that the following statements hold. 

\begin{enumerate}
 \item The dense-phase change-points are localized as                                      
 \[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \left| \hat{K}_1 - K_1 \right| \ \le \  4.1 \log n \right) = 1-o(1)
 \quad \text{ and } \quad 
 \left|\hat{K}_2 - K_2^{\star} \right| \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left( n p_n \log n \right).
 \] 
 \item The model parameters are consistently estimated:
 \[
 \frac{|\widehat p-p_n|}{p_n} \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}} \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{ n p_n } } \right),
  \quad 
 |\widehat\xi-\xi| = o_{\mathbb{P}}(1), 
 \quad 
 |\widehat\alpha-\alpha|
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}} \left( n^{1-\alpha} p_n \right).                                                                    
 \]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Localization and estimation from the exploration times

label: thm:weak_recovery
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weak_recovery}
Assume the conditions and notations of Theorem~\ref{thm:estimation}. Suppose in addition that the identities of the explored vertices $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{id}}$ are observed, and define $\widehat V_1 := \{u_k \colon \hat{K}_1 \ \le \  k \ < \ \hat{K}_2\}$. Then,
\[
\left| \widehat V_1 \cap V_0  \right| \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}} \left( n p_n \log n \right)
\quad \text{ and } \quad 
\left| \widehat V_1^c \cap V_1 \right| \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}} \left( n p_n \log n \right).
\]

label: lem:first-entry
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:first-entry}
Suppose $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $np_n\to\infty$. Set $K_1=\infty$ if the exploration never reaches $V_1$. Then
$\varepsilon_n:=\mathbb{P}(K_1=\infty)=o(1)$, and, for every
$k\in\mathbb N$,
\[
 \mathbb{P}(K_1>k)
 \ \le \  \left(1-\frac{n_1}{n}\right)^k+\varepsilon_n.
\]
In particular, for every sequence $f_n\to\infty$, we have 
$\mathbb{P}\bigl(K_1\le f_n n^{1-\alpha}\bigr)=1-o(1).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we show that $\varepsilon_n=o(1)$. 
Because $\xi\ge p_n$, we may couple the planted graph with a graph $H\sim G(n,p_n)$ such that every edge of $H$ is also present in the planted graph. 
Fix a vertex $v\in V_1$.
As $np_n\to\infty$, the graph $H$ has a unique giant component of size $n-o(n)$ with high probability. 
By exchangeability, both $v$ and the uniformly chosen source belong to this component with probability $1-o(1)$.  
They are therefore connected in the planted graph with probability $1-o(1)$, which proves $\varepsilon_n=o(1)$.

Next, extend the exploration by restarting from a uniformly
chosen unexplored vertex whenever its cut becomes empty.
Let $\widetilde K_1$ be the first index at which this extended
exploration visits $V_1$.

Before the first visit to $V_1$, no edge internal to $V_1$
can affect the exploration. Hence, the extended
exploration up to this visit has the same law as the
corresponding exploration on a Erd\H{o}s\xspace-R{\'e}nyi\xspace $G(n,p_n)$ graph.
In that graph, exchangeability of vertex labels, together
with the uniform source and restart rules, implies that the
full exploration order is a uniformly random permutation. 
                                                                        
It follows that, for $0\le k\le n-n_1$,
\[
    \mathbb{P}(\widetilde K_1>k)
    =\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}
        \left(1-\frac{n_1}{n-i}\right)
    \le \left(1-\frac{n_1}{n}\right)^k.
\]
For $k>n-n_1$, the left-hand side is zero, so the inequality
remains valid.

On the event $\{K_1<\infty\}$, the original exploration reaches $V_1$ before any restart occurs. Hence
$\widetilde K_1=K_1$ on this event, and therefore
\[
 \mathbb{P}(K_1>k) \ \le \  \mathbb{P}(\widetilde K_1>k)+\mathbb{P}(K_1=\infty),
\]
which proves the claimed bound.

Finally, take $k=\lfloor f_n n^{1-\alpha}\rfloor$.
Because $n_1/n^\alpha\to1$, we have $kn_1/n\to\infty$.
Thus
\[
 \mathbb{P}(K_1>k)
 \ \le \  \exp\left(-\frac{kn_1}{n}\right)+\varepsilon_n
 \ = \  o(1).
\]

 \xi D_k-\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}
 \ \le \  C_k 
 \ \le \  \xi D_k+\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}+U_k,
\]
with probability at least $1-n^{-2}-A_\eta n_1^{-\eta^2}$.

body_md:
\label{lem:PIT_plugin_stability}
Let $\varepsilon_n:=\left|\frac{\widehat p_n}{p_n}-1\right|$. 
Conditionally on \(\{\varepsilon_n<1\}\), we have 
\[
 \max_{1 \le k \le \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor } \left| \widehat Z_k-Z_k \right| \ \le \  \frac{\sqrt{12}}{e} \, \frac{\varepsilon_n}{1-\varepsilon_n}.
\]
In particular, for every collection of bins \(B_j \subseteq [1, \lfloor n / 2 \rfloor ] \),
\[
 \sup_j \left| \frac1{|B_j|}\sum_{k\in B_j}\widehat Z_k - \frac1{|B_j|}\sum_{k\in B_j}Z_k \right|
 \ \le \  \frac{\sqrt{12}}{e} \, \frac{\varepsilon_n}{1-\varepsilon_n}.
\]
head: environment
name: Stability of the probability integral transform

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $r_n:=\frac{\widehat p_n}{p_n}$ and $y_k:=m_k a_k\ge0$. 
Then $\widehat m_k a_k=r_n y_k$, and hence
\[
 |\widehat Z_k-Z_k|
 \ = \  \sqrt{12}\left|e^{-r_n y_k}-e^{-y_k}\right|.
\]
By the mean-value theorem, we have $\left|e^{-r_n y_k}-e^{-y_k}\right| = |r_n-1|\,y_k e^{-s y_k}$ for some $s \in [1, r_n]$.                                           
On the event \(\{|r_n-1|<1\}\), we have \(s\ge 1-\varepsilon_n\). Therefore
\[
 y_k e^{-s y_k}
 \ \le \  \sup_{y\ge0} \, y e^{-(1-\varepsilon_n)y}
 \ = \  \frac{1}{e(1-\varepsilon_n)}.
\]
Thus $|\widehat Z_k-Z_k| \le \frac{\sqrt{12}}{e} \frac{\varepsilon_n}{1-\varepsilon_n}$. Averaging over bins gives the second claim.

label: lem:p_hat_concentration
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:p_hat_concentration}
Let $\mathcal W\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ be a nonempty
deterministic index set, and write $M:=|\mathcal W|$.
Let $p>0$, and let $(X_k)_{k\in\mathcal W}$ be independent
exponential random variables with rates $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathcal W}$
satisfying
\[
    p\,k(n-k)(1-\varepsilon_-)
    \ \le \  \mu_k
    \ \le \  p\,k(n-k)(1+\varepsilon_+) 
    \qquad \forall k\in\mathcal W,
\]
for some $\varepsilon_-,\varepsilon_+\in[0,1)$.
Set $\varepsilon :=\max\left\{ \frac{\varepsilon_-}{1-\varepsilon_-}, \frac{\varepsilon_+}{1+\varepsilon_+} \right\}$ and define 
$\hat{p}_{{\rm MLE}\xspace} := \frac{M}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal W}k(n-k)X_k}.$ 
There exists an absolute constant $C>0$ such that, for every $x\ge0$ satisfying $\varepsilon+u(x)<1$, 
\[
 \frac{|\hat{p}_{{\rm MLE}\xspace}-p|}{p}
 \ \le \ 
 \frac{\varepsilon+u(x)}{1-\varepsilon-u(x)}.
\]
with probability at least $1-2e^{-x}$, where $u(x):=\frac{C}{1-\varepsilon_-} \left(\sqrt{\frac{x}{M}}+\frac{x}{M}\right)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\mathcal{S}_n := \left\{ \lceil n/3\rceil,\ldots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor \right\}$ and $m:=|\mathcal{S}_n|=\Theta(n).$ 
By Lemma~\ref{lem:post_dense_cut}~(ii), applied with $c_1=1/3$ and $c_2=1/2$, we have 
\[
 \varepsilon_n
 := \sup_{k\in\mathcal{S}_n} \left| \frac{C_k}{p_nk(n-k)}-1 \right|
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{np_n}}\right).
\]
In particular, $\varepsilon_n=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$.

Let $\mathcal J := \sigma\bigl(G,V_1,(u_k)_{k\ge1}\bigr).$ 
Conditionally on $\mathcal{J}$, the inter-arrival times $\{a_k:k\in\mathcal{S}_n\}$ are independent and satisfy $a_k \, | \, \mathcal{J} \sim\operatorname{Exp}(C_k).$ 
Moreover, on the event $\{\varepsilon_n<1\}$,
\[
 p_nk(n-k)(1-\varepsilon_n)
 \ \le \  C_k 
 \ \le \  p_nk(n-k)(1+\varepsilon_n)
\]
uniformly for $k\in\mathcal{S}_n$. 
By applying Lemma~\ref{lem:p_hat_concentration} conditionally on $\mathcal{J}$, we obtain 
\[
    \frac{|\widehat p-p_n|}{p_n}
    =
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(
        \varepsilon_n+\frac1{\sqrt n}
    \right).
\]
Because $p_n\le1$, we have $\frac1{\sqrt n} \le \frac1{\sqrt{np_n}}$. 
We conclude using $\varepsilon_n = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\frac1{\sqrt{np_n}}\right)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the reference set $V_1^\star:=\{u_k:K_1\le k<K_2^\star\}.$ 
Because $K_2^\star-K_1=n_1=|V_1|$, we have $|V_1^\star|=|V_1|$.
Moreover, the number of vertices of $V_0$ contained in $V_1^\star$ is at most the total number of $V_0$-vertices explored between $K_1$ and the full exploration of $V_1$, namely $K_2-K_2^\star$. Hence
\[
 |V_1\triangle V_1^\star|
 \ = \  2|V_1^\star\cap V_0|
 \ \le \  2(K_2-K_2^\star).
\]
Furthermore, because we defined $\widehat V_1=\{u_k:\widehat K_1\le k<\widehat K_2\}$, 
the symmetric difference between the estimated and reference intervals satisfies
\[
 |\widehat V_1\triangle V_1^\star|
 \ \le \  |\widehat K_1-K_1| + |\widehat K_2-K_2^\star|.
\]
Therefore,
\[
 |V_1\triangle\widehat V_1|
 \ \le \  2(K_2-K_2^\star) + |\widehat K_1-K_1| + |\widehat K_2-K_2^\star|.
\]
By Propositions~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd},
\ref{prop:K1_detection}, and~\ref{prop:K2_detection}, we obtain 
$|V_1\triangle\widehat V_1| = O_{\mathbb{P}}(np_n\log n).$
Because both $|\widehat V_1\cap V_0|$ and $|\widehat V_1^c\cap V_1|$ are bounded by $|V_1\triangle\widehat V_1|$, the claimed bounds follow.

title: Proof
body_md:
Condition on the source $u_1$. As $d_n := np_n \to\infty$, we have $\delta_n:= \sqrt{\frac{24\log(e d_n)}{d_n}}<1$ for all sufficiently large $n$. 

Fix a deterministic set $S$ containing $u_1$ such that $k := |S|\le n/2$, and let $\mu_k=p_nk(n-k)$. 
Define the two events
\[
    A_S:=\{G[S]\text{ is connected}\}
    \quad \text{ and } \quad 
    B_S:=\bigl\{
        \bigl||\operatorname{Cut}(S)|-\mu_k\bigr|
        >\delta_n\mu_k
    \bigr\}.
\]
The event $A_S$ depends only on edges internal to $S$, whereas
$B_S$ depends only on edges between $S$ and its complement.
These edge families are disjoint and $S$ was chosen independent of $G$, so $A_S$ and $B_S$ are independent.

There are $k(n-k)$ possible crossing edges, each present independently with probability~$p_n$. Thus $|\operatorname{Cut}(S)|\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k(n-k),p_n)$.
The multiplicative Chernoff bound, together with $\mu_k\ge d_n k/2$, gives
\[
 \mathbb{P}(B_S)
 \ \le \  2\exp\left(-\frac{\delta_n^2\mu_k}{3}\right)
 \ \le \  2\exp\left(-\frac{\delta_n^2 d_n k}{6}\right).
\]

For $k\ge2$, connectivity requires the presence of a spanning tree.
Rooting such a tree at $u_1$ assigns a parent to each of the other
$k-1$ vertices, so there are at most $k^{k-1}$ possible trees.
Each tree has $k-1$ edges and is present with probability $p_n^{k-1}$.
A union bound therefore yields $\mathbb{P}(A_S)\le k^{k-1}p_n^{k-1}.$ 

By independence of $A_S$ and $B_S$, we obtain
\[
 \mathbb{P}(A_S\cap B_S)
 \ \le \  2k^{k-1}p_n^{k-1} \exp\left(-\frac{\delta_n^2 d_n k}{6}\right).
\]

There are $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ sets of size $k$ containing $u_1$, and
\[
 \binom{n-1}{k-1}k^{k-1}p_n^{k-1}
 \ \le \  (ed_n)^{k-1} \left(\frac{k}{k-1}\right)^{k-1}
 \ \le \  e(ed_n)^{k-1}.
\]
Hence, a union bound over all these sets and their sizes gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left( \bigcup_{k=2}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} \ \bigcup_{\substack{S \colon u_1 \in S, \\ |S|=k}} (A_S\cap B_S) \right) 
 & \ \le \  2e\sum_{k=2}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor} (ed_n)^{k-1} \exp\left(-\frac{\delta_n^2d_nk}{6}\right)\\
 & \ \le \  2e\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}(ed_n)^{-3k-1}
 \ = \  o(1),
\end{align*}
where the second inequality uses $\delta_n^2 d_n/6=4\log(ed_n)$.
For $k=1$, the only set is $\{u_1\}$, and the same Chernoff bound gives $\mathbb{P}(B_{\{u_1\}})\le2(ed_n)^{-4}=o(1)$.

It follows that, with probability $1-o(1)$, every connected set $S$ containing $u_1$ and with $|S|\le n/2$ satisfies
\[
 \left| \frac{|\operatorname{Cut}(S)|}{p_n|S|(n-|S|)}-1 \right|
 \ \le \  \delta_n.
\]
We conclude as $\mathcal{I}_k$ contains $u_1$ and has cardinality $k \le n/2$.

name: Lower bound on the conditional probability of activating a $V_1$-vertex

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H = \{K_1\le n^{1-\alpha}\log n\}$ and write $\mathbb{P}_H(\cdot):=\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid H)$ and $\mathbb{E}_H[\cdot]:=\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid H]$. 
As~$H$ is $\mathcal{F}_{K_1}$-measurable, conditioning on $H$ preserves the conditional transition probabilities after $K_1$, that is, $\mathbb{P}_H(u_{k+1}\in V_1\mid\mathcal{F}_k) = \mathbb{P}(u_{k+1}\in V_1\mid\mathcal{F}_k)$ for all $k\ge K_1$.

Let $\mathcal E$ be the event on which the uniform cut bounds used in Lemma~\ref{lm:lower-bound-prujF} hold. 
Because $\mathbb{P}(H)=1-o(1)$, these bounds give $\mathbb{P}_H(\mathcal E^c)\le C_0n^{-c_0}$ for some constants $C_0,c_0>0$. 
Let $k\le n/2$ and $i:=I_1(k)\in\{1,\ldots,n_1-1\}$. On $\mathcal{E}$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dense-transition-bound}
 \mathbb{P}(u_{k+1}\in V_1\mid\mathcal{F}_k)
 \ \ge \  \left( 1+C_1\frac{d_nk+\log n}{i(n_1-i)} \right)^{-1}.
\end{equation}
This also ensures that the cut is positive while $V_1$ remains partially explored.

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{(i) Early regime.}
Set $m:=m_n$. Before the first outside exploration, when exactly
$i$ vertices of $V_1$ have been explored, we have $k=K_1+i-1$.
For $1\le i<m$, using $m=o(n_1)$, on $\mathcal{E}$ Equation~\eqref{eq:dense-transition-bound} therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb{P}(u_{K_1+i}\in V_0\mid\mathcal{F}_{K_1+i-1})
 \ \le \  C\left( \frac{d_nK_1+\log n}{in_1} + \frac{d_n}{n_1} \right). 
\]

For the auxiliary exploration that restarts uniformly whenever its cut vanishes, the first-entry index $\widetilde K_1$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K_1]=\frac{n+1}{n_1+1}.$\footnote{Indeed, in a $G_{n,{p_n}}$, label symmetry and uniform restarts make the exploration order a uniform random permutation. Therefore \(\widetilde K_1\) has the distribution of the position of the first vertex of \(V_1\) in such a permutation. The \(n-n_1\) other vertices occupy \(n_1+1\) exchangeable gaps: before, between, and after the vertices of \(V_1\). Each gap has expected size \((n-n_1)/(n_1+1)\). Because \(\widetilde K_1\) is one plus the first gap’s size, we obtain
$\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K_1] = 1+\frac{n-n_1}{n_1+1} = \frac{n+1}{n_1+1}.$}
Moreover, $\widetilde K_1=K_1$ on $H$. Hence,
\[
 \mathbb{E}_H[K_1]
 \ \le \  \frac{\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K_1]}{\mathbb{P}(H)}
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}(n/n_1).
\]

For $1\le i<m$, let $A_i$ be the event that the first $i$ explorations starting at $K_1$ are finite and belong to $V_1$, and that the cut bounds hold at step $K_1+i-1$.
Then $A_i$ is $\mathcal{F}_{K_1+i-1}$-measurable. Using the preceding bound on the probability of exploring $V_0$ next, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}_H\bigl(A_i\cap\{u_{K_1+i}\in V_0\}\bigr) 
 & \ = \  \mathbb{E}_H\left[ \mathbf1_{A_i} \mathbb{P}(u_{K_1+i}\in V_0\mid\mathcal{F}_{K_1+i-1}) \right] \\
 &\ \le \  C\,\mathbb{E}_H\left[ \mathbf1_{A_i} \left( \frac{d_nK_1+\log n}{in_1} + \frac{d_n}{n_1} \right) \right] \\
 &\ \le \  C\left( \frac{d_n\mathbb{E}_H[K_1]+\log n}{in_1} + \frac{d_n}{n_1} \right).
\end{align*}
For sufficiently large $n$, we have $m<n_1$.
On $\mathcal E$, extinction is impossible while the explored vertices of $V_1$ number between $1$ and $m-1$.
Thus, if the first $m$ explorations starting at $K_1$ are not all finite and in $V_1$, then either $\mathcal E$ fails or a first outside exploration occurs after $i$ consecutive vertices of $V_1$, for some $1\le i<m$.
A union bound therefore gives
\begin{align}
 &\mathbb{P}_H\bigl( \text{the first $m$ explorations starting at $K_1$ are not all finite and in $V_1$ }
    \bigr) \nonumber
    \\
    &\quad\le
    \mathbb{P}_H(\mathcal E^c)
    +\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}
      \mathbb{P}_H\bigl(A_i\cap\{u_{K_1+i}\in V_0\}\bigr) \nonumber
    \\
    &\quad\le
    \mathbb{P}_H(\mathcal E^c)
    +C\left[
        \frac{d_n\mathbb{E}_H[K_1]+\log n}{n_1}\log(m+1)
        +\frac{d_nm}{n_1}
    \right] \nonumber \\
    & \ \le \  C_0n^{-c_0}
    +C\left[
        \left(\frac{d_nn}{n_1^2}+\frac{\log n}{n_1}\right)
        \log(m+1)
        +\frac{d_nm}{n_1}
    \right], \label{eq:in_proof}
\end{align}
where we used $\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}i^{-1}\le C\log(m+1)$, and $\mathbb{E}_H[K_1]=O(n/n_1)$ and
$\mathbb{P}_H(\mathcal E^c)\le C_0n^{-c_0}$.

The right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:in_proof} tends to zero, because $\frac{d_nn}{n_1^2}\log(m+1) =O\left(\frac{d_n\log n}{n^{2\alpha-1}}\right)=o(1)$, $\frac{\log n\log(m+1)}{n_1}=o(1)$ and $\frac{d_nm}{n_1}=o(1).$ 
This proves (i). 

\medskip
\noindent
\textit{(ii) Bulk regime.}
Let $S$ be the total number of outside explorations after $K_1$
and before completing $V_1$, with $S=\infty$ if completion never
occurs. Fix a constant $A>0$, to be chosen sufficiently large,
and set
$M:=\lceil A d_n\log n\rceil.$ 
Stop the comparison at completion of $V_1$, the first failure of
a current cut bound, or the $(M+1)$-st outside exploration.
Before stopping,
\[
 k \ \le \  K_1+n_1+M \ \le \  3n_1 \ < \ n/2
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$.
Thus \eqref{eq:dense-transition-bound} gives the lower success
probabilities
\[
    q_i:=
    \left(
        1+L\frac{d_nn_1}{i(n_1-i)}
    \right)^{-1},
    \qquad 1\le i\le n_1-1,
\]
where $L>0$ can be chosen independently of the fixed constant $A$.

Using fresh independent uniform sequences for the successive trials in each stage $i$, couple the exploration with independent variables
$\widetilde G_i\sim\operatorname{Geom}(q_i)-1.$ 
Up to stopping, the number of outside explorations in each stage, including any partially completed stage, is at most~$\widetilde G_i$.
On $\mathcal E$, extinction before completion is impossible.
Therefore, reaching $M+1$ outside explorations forces $\sum_i\widetilde G_i>M$, and hence
\[
    \mathbb{P}_H(S>M)
    \ \le \ 
    C_0n^{-c_0}
    +
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \sum_{i=1}^{n_1-1}\widetilde G_i>M
    \right).
\]
Moreover, 
\[
 \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_i \tilde{G}_i \right]
\ = \  \sum_{i=1}^{n_1-1}\frac{1-q_i}{q_i}
 \ = \  Ld_nn_1\sum_{i=1}^{n_1-1}\frac1{i(n_1-i)}
 \ = \  2Ld_n\sum_{i=1}^{n_1-1}\frac1i
 \ \asymp \  d_n\log n,
\]
where we used $\frac1{i(n_1-i)} = \frac1{n_1}\left(\frac1i+\frac1{n_1-i}\right).$
Therefore, Lemma~\ref{lm:geom_sum_concentration} applied with $q_\ast:=\min_{1\le i\le n_1-1}q_i\ge\frac{c_1}{d_n}$ and with $A$ sufficiently large, gives $\mathbb{P}\left( \sum_{i=1}^{n_1-1}\widetilde G_i>M \right)
 \le n^{-c_2}$ for some $c_2>0$.
After adjusting constants, we obtain
\[
    \mathbb{P}_H(S\le Cd_n\log n) \ \ge \  1-n^{-c}
\]
for some $c,C>0$. 
On this event, before completion of $V_1$,
\[
    I_1(K_1-1+j)\ \ge \  j-S\ \ge \  j-Cd_n\log n.
\]
After completion, $I_1=n_1$. 
This proves the uniform bound in (ii).
Finally, completion occurs at index $K_1+n_1-1+S$, so $K_2-K_2^\star = S \le Cd_n\log n$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $G[V_1]$ is the subgraph induced by $V_1$.  For $S\subseteq V_1$, define the set of edges of the induced subgraph $G[V_1]$ crossing from $S$ to $V_1\setminus S$ by 
\[
 \operatorname{Cut}_{G[V_1]}(S)
 := \bigl\{ \{u,v\}\in E(G[V_1]) \colon u\in S,\ v\in V_1\setminus S \bigr\}. 
\]

We decompose the cut $C_k = | \operatorname{Cut}(\mathcal{I}_k) |$ after $k$ explored vertices as 
$C_k \ = \  C_k^{\mathrm{in}}+C_k^{\mathrm{out}},$ 
where $C_k^{\mathrm{in}} := \left| \operatorname{Cut}_{G[V_1]}(I_k\cap V_1) \right|$  is the contribution of cut edges internal to $V_1$, and $C_k^{\mathrm{out}}:=C_k-C_k^{\mathrm{in}}$ contains all remaining cut edges.

\medskip\noindent
\textit{(i) Internal dense contribution.}
The induced graph $G[V_1]$ is distributed as $G(n_1,\xi)$.

If $\xi<1$, then, because $\xi$ is fixed, we have $\xi(1-\xi)n_1\gg\log n_1,$ and the assumptions of Lemma~\ref{lm:dense_cut_conc} hold for sufficiently large $n$. 
Applying that lemma to $G[V_1]$, there exists a constant $A_\eta<\infty$ such that, with probability at least $1-A_\eta n_1^{-\eta^2}$, simultaneously for every subset $S\subseteq V_1$, $1\leq |S|\leq n_1-1$,
\begin{align*}
 &\left| \operatorname{Cut}_{G[V_1]}(S) - \xi |S|(n_1-|S|) \right| \\
 & \ \le \  (1+\eta)  \sqrt{ 2\xi(1-\xi) |S|(n_1-|S|) \min\{|S|, n_1-|S|\}\log\left( \frac{e n_1}{\min\{|S|, n_1-|S|\}} \right) },
\end{align*}

As this bound holds simultaneously for all subsets of $V_1$, we can apply it to the random set $S=\mathcal{I}_k\cap V_1$. 
Moreover, observe that, for $M_k\ge1$, we have $\log\left(\frac{e n_1}{M_k}\right) \ \le \  \log(en_1).$ 
Thus, we obtain, simultaneously for all $k$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:in_proof_cut_all_phase}
 \left| C_k^{\mathrm{in}}-\xi D_k \right| \ \le \  \Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}.
\end{align} 

If $\xi=1$, the graph induced by $V_1$ is complete, so $C_k^{\mathrm{in}}=D_k$ and the bound~\eqref{eq:in_proof_cut_all_phase} holds with $\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}=0$.

Denote by $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{in}}$ the event $ \left| C_k^{\mathrm{in}}-\xi D_k \right| \ \le \  \Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}$. We just established that 
$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{in}}^c)
 \le A_\eta n_1^{-\eta^2}.$

\smallskip \noindent
\textit{(ii) Sparse contribution.}
We condition on $V_1$ and let $X_i$ be the random variable counting the number of edges from $u_i$ to $\mathcal{I}_i^c$ excluding pairs contained in $V_1$. 
Conditioned on the exploration history just before $u_i$ is explored, the edge-indicators from $u_i$ to $\mathcal{I}_i^c$ but excluding pairs contained in $V_1$ are independent $\operatorname{Ber}(p_n)$ variables, and there are at most $n$ of them. 
Hence, $X_i \le Z_i$ where $Z_i \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n,p_n)$.
Moreover, because $Z_i$ involves only edges incident to~$u_i$, and because the vertices $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ are distinct, the random variables $Z_1,\ldots,Z_k$ can be constructed to be mutually independent, and thus $\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i \sim \operatorname{Bin}(kn,p_n)$.
Because every edge in $C_k^{\mathrm{out}}$ was first counted in some $X_i$ with $i \le k$, we obtain 
\[
    C_k^{\mathrm{out}} \ \preceq_{\text{st}} \ \sum_{i=1}^k X_i \ \preceq_{\text{st}} \ \sum_{i=1}^k Z_i \ \sim \  \operatorname{Bin}( kn, p_n).
\]
Bernstein's inequality gives $\mathbb{P}(C_k^{\mathrm{out}} > p_nkn + \sqrt{6p_nkn\log n} + \log n) \le n^{-3}$. A union bound over $1\le k\le n/2$ therefore yields an event $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{out}}$ for which $C_k^{\mathrm{out}} \le U_k$ for all $1\le k\le n/2$, and such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{out}}^c) \le \frac{1}{2}n^{-2}$.  

\medskip\noindent 
\textit{Conclusion.} We conclude by considering the event $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{in}}\cap\mathcal E_{\mathrm{out}}$.

body_md:
\label{lemma:homogeneous-cut-upper}
Consider the sequence $(C_1,\cdots,C_n)$ of cut-sizes of a continuous FPP process with rate $\lambda=1$ in a $G_{n,{p_n}}$ graph. 
For every $1\le k\le n-1$,  
\[
    C_k \ \preceq_{\text{st}} \ \operatorname{Bin}(k(n-k),p_n).

name: Stochastic upper bound

title: Proof
body_md:
Compare the FPP exploration with an auxiliary exploration on $G(n,p)$ that selects each next vertex uniformly from the unexplored vertices, independently of the graph. 
Its explored set $\mathcal J_k$ has size $k$ and is independent of the graph, so its cut size satisfies
\[
 C_k^+:=|\operatorname{Cut}(\mathcal J_k)|
 \sim \operatorname{Bin}(k(n-k),p).
\]
We couple the two explorations by revealing edges only when one of
their endpoints is explored.

After $k$ steps, let $x_1\le\cdots\le x_m$ and $y_1\le\cdots\le y_m$, where $m=n-k$, be the ordered numbers of explored neighbors of the remaining vertices in the FPP and auxiliary explorations, respectively. 
Observe that $C_k =\sum_{i=1}^m x_i$ and $C^+_k =\sum_{i=1}^m y_i.$

It remains to be shown that there exists a coupling such that $x_i\le y_i$ for every $i$.
Initially, couple these sequences to be equal. Suppose inductively
that $x_i\le y_i$ for every $i$ and that $\sum_i x_i>0$.
The FPP exploration selects a rank $R$ with probabilities proportional
to the $x_i$, whereas the auxiliary exploration selects a uniform
rank $U$. Since the $x_i$ are nondecreasing,
\[
    \mathbb{P}(R\le r\mid x_1,\ldots,x_m)
    =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^r x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^m x_i}
    \le \frac{r}{m},
    \qquad 1\le r\le m.
\]
Thus $R$ and $U$ can be coupled so that $R\ge U$.

Deleting $x_R$ and $y_U$ preserves the coordinatewise ordering
of the remaining ordered sequences. Indeed, between the two deleted
ranks, the new comparison is $x_i\le y_{i+1}$; elsewhere the original
comparisons remain valid. The edges from each newly selected vertex
to its remaining unexplored vertices have not yet been revealed.
Their indicators are fresh independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables.
Couple these indicators coordinatewise in the two explorations.
Adding the same indicators and then reordering preserves the
coordinatewise inequality.

Induction gives $C_k\le C_k^+$ until the FPP exploration stops.
Afterward, $C_k=0\le C_k^+$ by convention. The claimed stochastic
domination follows.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:dense_cut_conc}
Let $G \sim G_{n,{p_n}}$, let $\eta>0$, and assume that either
$p(1-p)n \ge C_\eta \log(en)$, with $C_\eta:=\frac{(1+\eta)^2(1+\eta^2)^2}{\eta^2}$, or $p=1$. 
For $S \subseteq V(G)$, let $m(S):=\min\{|S|,n-|S|\}$. Then, with probability at least $1 - 2\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{k}^{-\eta^2}$, we have simultaneously for all $S\subseteq V$ that
\[
\left| \operatorname{Cut}(S) - p|S|(n-|S|) \right|
\ \le \  (1+\eta)\sqrt{ 2p(1-p)|S|(n-|S|) \log\binom{n}{m(S)}}.
\]
Moreover, for every fixed $\eta>0$, there is a constant $A_\eta<\infty$ such that $2\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{k}^{-\eta^2} < A_{\eta} n^{-\eta^2}$.

body_md:
Denote by $C_k^{\mathrm{in}}$ and $C_k^{\mathrm{out}}$ the numbers of cut edges whose unexplored endpoints belong to $V_1$ and $V_0$, respectively. 
Let $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{dense}}$ be the event that
\[
 \bigl|\operatorname{Cut}_{G[V_1]}(S)\bigr|
 \ \ge \  \frac{\xi}{2}|S|(n_1-|S|)
 \qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V_1.
\]
As $\xi>0$ is fixed and $n_1=\lfloor n^\alpha\rfloor$, Lemma~\ref{lm:dense_cut_conc} implies, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
    \mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{dense}}^c)\le Cn^{-c}
\]
for some constants $c,C>0$.
When $\xi=1$, this event holds deterministically.

The sparse-cut bound established in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:G_npbx_cut_bound} gives an event
$\mathcal E_{\mathrm{out}}$, with
$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{out}}^c)\le \frac12 n^{-2}$,
on which, simultaneously for every $k\le n/2$ with $t_k<\infty$,
\[
 C_k^{\mathrm{out}}
 \ \le \  U_k :=p_nkn+\sqrt{6p_nkn\log n}+\log n.
\]
Indeed, $C_k^{\mathrm{out}}$ is bounded by the full sparse contribution considered there.

Set $\mathcal{E} := \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{dense}}\cap\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{out}}.$ 
After adjusting constants, we have $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^c)\le C_0n^{-c}$.

We now work on $\mathcal{E}$, and fix $k\le n/2$ with $t_k<\infty$ and $1\le i:=I_1(k)\le n_1-1$. Every internal dense edge crossing from $I_k\cap V_1$ to $V_1\setminus I_k$ contributes to $C_k^{\mathrm{in}}$.
Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:in_proof_lowerbound_Ckin}
 C_k^{\mathrm{in}}
 \ \ge \  \bigl|\operatorname{Cut}_{G[V_1]}(I_k\cap V_1)\bigr|
 \ \ge \  \frac{\xi}{2}i(n_1-i) \ > \ 0.
\end{equation}
Moreover, using $k\le n/2$ and $\sqrt{6x\log n}\le x+\frac32\log n$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:in_proof_lowerbound_Ckout}
 C_k^{\mathrm{out}}
 \ \le \  2p_nkn+\frac52\log n
 \ \le \  4\bigl(p_nk(n-k)+\log n\bigr).
\end{equation}

By the memorylessness of the exponential exploration times, the next exploration edge is uniform among the current edges belonging to the cut.
Combining \eqref{eq:in_proof_lowerbound_Ckin} and \eqref{eq:in_proof_lowerbound_Ckout}, we therefore obtain
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}(u_{k+1}\in V_1\mid\mathcal{F}_k)
 \ = \  \frac{C_k^{\mathrm{in}}}{C_k^{\mathrm{in}}+C_k^{\mathrm{out}}}
 & \ \ge \  \left( 1+\frac{8}{\xi} \frac{p_nk(n-k)+\log n}{i(n_1-i)} \right)^{-1}\\
 & \ \ge \  1-\frac{8}{\xi} \frac{p_nk(n-k)+\log n}{i(n_1-i)},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality uses $(1+x)^{-1}\ge1-x$ for $x\ge0$.
All bounds hold simultaneously over the stated range of $k$,
which proves the lemma.

label: eq:post_dense_fixed_set_cut
title: Proof
body_md:
The two statements (i) and (ii) rely on the same observation. 
Condition on the planted set $V_1$, and fix a deterministic set $S\subseteq V$ such that $V_1\subseteq S$. 
Because all vertices of $V_1$ belong to $S$, the edges belonging to $\operatorname{Cut}(S)$ each have at most one endpoint in $V_1$. 
Therefore, all potential edges between vertices in $S$ and vertices in $V\setminus S$ are independent $\operatorname{Ber}(p_n)$ variables, and 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:post_dense_fixed_set_cut}
 |\operatorname{Cut}(S)| \sim \operatorname{Bin}\bigl(|S|(n-|S|),p_n\bigr).
\end{equation}
To prove (i) and (ii), we use this fact over two different families of sets.

\medskip \noindent \emph{Proof of (i).}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:first-entry} and Proposition~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd}, there exists a constant $C>0$
such that the event
$\mathcal E_n := \left\{ K_1\le n^{1-\alpha}\log n \text{ and } \ 0\le K_2-K_2^\star\le Cnp_n\log n \right\}$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_n)=1-o(1)$.

We work on this event $\mathcal E_n$. 
As $K_2$ is the first exploration index after all vertices of $V_1$ have been explored, we have $V_1\subseteq\mathcal I_k$ for every $k \ge K_2$. 
Moreover, for $K_2 \le k \le K_2+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil,$ using $K_2^\star=K_1+n_1$ and the definition of $\mathcal{E}_n$, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
 |\mathcal I_k\setminus V_1|
 \ = \  k-n_1
 \ \le \  K_2-n_1+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil 
 \ \le \  m_n, 
\end{align*}
where we defined $m_n := \left\lceil n^{1-\alpha}\log n + (B+C+1)np_n\log n \right\rceil.$
Because $\alpha>1/2$ and $np_n\log n=o(n_1)$, we have $m_n=o(n_1)$. 

We introduce 
\[
 \mathcal{S}_n := \left\{ S\subseteq V\colon V_1\subseteq S \text{ and } |S\setminus V_1|\le m_n \right\}.
\]
For any $S\in\mathcal{S}_n$, because $m_n=o(n_1)$ and $n_1=o(n)$, we have $|S|=(1+o(1))n_1$ and $n-|S|=(1-o(1))n$, uniformly in $S$. Hence, writing $\mu_S:=p_n|S|(n-|S|),$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:post_dense_local_mean}
 \inf_{S\in\mathcal{S}_n}\mu_S \ \ge \  c(np_n)n_1
\end{equation}
for some constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$.


Next, we upper-bound the size of $\mathcal{S}_n$. 
Because only vertices of $V_0$ may be added to $V_1$, we have  $|\mathcal{S}_n| \le \sum_{j=0}^{m_n}\binom{n}{j},$ 
and hence, for some constant $C'>0$,
$\log|\mathcal{S}_n| \le C'm_n\log\left(\frac{en}{m_n}\right).$ 
Using the definition of $m_n$,
\[
    m_n\log\left(\frac{en}{m_n}\right)
    =
    O\left(
        n^{1-\alpha}\log^2 n
        +
        np_n\log^2 n
    \right).
\]
Dividing by $(np_n)n_1\asymp(np_n)n^\alpha$, and using $\alpha>1/2$ and $np_n\gg 1$ gives
\[
 \frac{ n^{1-\alpha}\log^2 n }{ (np_n)n^\alpha }
 = \frac{ n^{1-2\alpha}\log^2 n }{ np_n }
 =o(1)
 \quad \text{and} \quad 
 \frac{ np_n\log^2 n }{ (np_n)n^\alpha }
 = \frac{\log^2 n}{n^\alpha}
 =o(1).
\]
Therefore, 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:local_post_dense_entropy}
 \log|\mathcal{S}_n|
 \ = \  o\bigl((np_n)n_1\bigr).
\end{equation}

Choose a deterministic strictly positive and vanishing sequence $\varepsilon_n = o(1)$ such that $\varepsilon_n^2(np_n)n_1 \gg \log|\mathcal{S}_n|.$ 
For every fixed $S\in\mathcal{S}_n$, Chernoff bounds give
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \bigg| |\operatorname{Cut}(S)|-\mu_S \bigg| > \varepsilon_n\mu_S \right)
 \ \le \  2\exp\left\{ -c\varepsilon_n^2\mu_S \right\}
\]
for some constant $c>0$. 
Using~\eqref{eq:post_dense_local_mean}, \eqref{eq:local_post_dense_entropy}, and a union bound over $S\in\mathcal{S}_n$, yields
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \sup_{S\in\mathcal{S}_n} \left| \frac{|\operatorname{Cut}(S)|}{p_n|S|(n-|S|)} - 1 \right| > \varepsilon_n \right)
 \ = \  o(1).
\]

Finally, on the event~$\mathcal{E}_n$, every exploration set $\mathcal I_k$ with $K_2\le k\le K_2+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil$ belongs to $\mathcal{S}_n$. Hence, taking $S=\mathcal I_k$ in the preceding uniform estimate therefore proves 
\[
 \sup_{ K_2\le k\le K_2+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil } \left| \frac{C_k}{p_nk(n-k)}-1 \right|
 \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(1). 
\]

\medskip \noindent 
\emph{Proof of (ii).}
Because $K_1=o_{\mathbb{P}}(n)$, $n_1=o(n)$, and $np_n\log n=o(n_1)$, we have 
\[
    K_2
    =
    K_2^\star+\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np_n\log n)
    =
    K_1+n_1+\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np_n\log n)
    =
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(n),
\]
Hence $\mathbb{P}(K_2<c_1n) = 1-o(1).$
On this event $\{ K_2 < c_1 n \}$, we have 
\[
    V_1\subseteq\mathcal I_k
    \qquad
    \text{for all }
    \lceil c_1n\rceil\le k\le\lfloor c_2n\rfloor.
\]

Consider
\[
 \mathcal{S}_n := \left\{ S\subseteq V \colon V_1\subseteq S \text{ and } c_1n\le |S|\le c_2n \right\}.
\]
For every $S\in\mathcal{S}_n$, \eqref{eq:post_dense_fixed_set_cut} holds and
\[
 \mu_S := p_n|S|(n-|S|)
 \ \ge \  c_1(1-c_2)p_nn^2
 \ = \  c_1(1-c_2)n(np_n).
\]
Moreover, $|\mathcal{S}_n|\le2^n.$ 
Let $\varepsilon_n:=\frac{M}{\sqrt{np_n}},$ where $M>0$ is a fixed constant. 
Because $np_n\to\infty$, we have $\varepsilon_n<1$ for all sufficiently large $n$. 
Again by Chernoff bounds,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\left( \sup_{S\in\mathcal{S}_n} \left| \frac{|\operatorname{Cut}(S)|}{p_n|S|(n-|S|)}-1 \right| > \frac{M}{\sqrt{np_n}} \right)
& \ \le \  2^n\, 2\exp\left\{ - c' \frac{M^2}{np_n} c_1(1-c_2)n(np_n) \right\} \\
& \ = \  2\exp\left\{ n\left( \log2-c'c_1(1-c_2)M^2 \right) \right\}.
\end{align*}
Choosing $M$ sufficiently large makes the last expression tend to
zero exponentially fast.  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{S\in\mathcal{S}_n} \left| \frac{|\operatorname{Cut}(S)|}{p_n|S|(n-|S|)}-1 \right|
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{np_n}}\right).
\]
We conclude by noticing that $\mathcal{I}_k\in\mathcal{S}_n$ for every $c_1n\le k\le c_2n$, a.a.s.

label: lm:geom_sum_concentration
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:geom_sum_concentration}
Let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) be independent random variables with $G_i\sim \operatorname{Geom}(q_i)-1$, where \(q_i\in(0,1]\). Let $q_*:=\min_{i\in[m]}q_i$ and $\mu:=\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{1-q_i}{q_i}$. 
Then, for every \(M>3/2\), 
\[ 
 \mathbb{P}\left( \sum_{i=1}^m G_i\ge M\mu \right)
 \ \le \  \exp\left( -\frac{(2M-3)}{12}q_*\mu \right).
\]
head: environment
name: Concentration for sums of geometric random variables

title: Proof
body_md:
If \(\mu=0\), then \(q_i=1\) for every \(i\), and hence \(G_i=0\) almost surely for every \(i\). The claim is then trivial.
We may therefore assume that \(\mu>0\).  
Recall that, for \(G_i\sim \operatorname{Geom}(q_i)-1\), 
\[
 \mathbb{E}\left[e^{\lambda G_i}\right]
 \ = \  \sum_{k=0}^\infty q_i(1-q_i)^k e^{\lambda k}
 \ = \  \frac{q_i}{1-(1-q_i)e^\lambda},
\]
provided $(1-q_i)e^\lambda<1$ or, equivalently, whenever $\lambda<-\log(1-q_i)$.

Let $0 < \lambda < -\log(1-q_*)$. 
By Chernoff's bound and independence,
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m G_i\ge M\mu\right)
 \ \le \  e^{-\lambda M\mu} \prod_{i=1}^m \mathbb{E} e^{\lambda G_i} 
 \ = \  e^{-\lambda M\mu} \prod_{i=1}^m \frac{q_i}{1-(1-q_i)e^\lambda}.
\]
Rewrite each factor as
\[
 \frac{q_i}{1-(1-q_i)e^\lambda} \ = \  \frac{1}{1-x_i}
 \qquad \text{ where }     x_i:=\frac{(1-q_i)(e^\lambda-1)}{q_i}.
\]
Let $\lambda = \log(1+\theta q_*)$ where $\theta\in(0,1)$. Observe that this choice of $\lambda$ is admissible, since 
$
 e^{\lambda} \ = \  1+\theta q_* \ \le \  1+q_* \ \le \  \frac{1}{1-q_*}. 
$ 
With this choice of $\lambda$, we get
\begin{align*}
 x_i \ = \  \frac{1-q_i}{q_i} \theta q_* \ \le \  \theta(1-q_i) \ \le \  \theta. 
\end{align*}
Thus,
\begin{align*}
 \log \frac{1}{1-x_i} 
 \ \le \  \frac{x_i}{1-x_i}
 \ \le \  \frac{x_i}{1-\theta}
 \ = \  \frac{\theta q_*}{1-\theta} \frac{1-q_i}{q_i}. 
\end{align*}
Because $\mu = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1-q_i}{q_i}$, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m G_i\ge M\mu\right)
 & \ \le \  \exp\left( - \lambda M \mu + \frac{\theta}{1-\theta} q_* \mu \right).
\end{align*}
Using $\log(1+x) \ge x/(1+x)$ valid for $x \ge 0$, we finally obtain 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m G_i\ge M\mu\right)
 & \ \le \  \exp\left( - \left( \frac{M\theta}{1+\theta} - \frac{\theta}{1-\theta} \right) q_* \mu  \right).
\end{align*}
We conclude by taking $\theta=1/5$.

label: lemma:FP_bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:FP_bound}
Let $(\mathcal{F}_k)_{k\ge1}$ be a filtration, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_\kappa$ be random variables such that $Z_k$ is $\mathcal{F}_{k+1}$-measurable and takes values in $[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3]$.
Write $b_k:=\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]$.
Fix an integer $1\le w\le\kappa$, and let $S$ be a stopping time taking values in $\{1,\ldots,\kappa-w+1\}$. Define $\overline Z_S:=\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}Z_{S+r}.$ 
For any event $\mathcal E$, the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)]
    If, on $\mathcal E$, we have $b_{S+r}\le\delta$ for every
    $0\le r<w$, then, for every $H>\delta$,
    \[
        \mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathcal E\cap\{\overline Z_S>H\}\bigr)
        \le
        \exp\left\{-\frac{w(H-\delta)^2}{6}\right\}.
    \]

    \item[(ii)]
    If, on $\mathcal E$, we have $b_{S+r}\ge z$ for every
    $0\le r<w$, then, for every $H<z$,
    \[
        \mathbb{P}\bigl(\mathcal E\cap\{\overline Z_S\le H\}\bigr)
        \le
        \exp\left\{-\frac{w(z-H)^2}{6}\right\}.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, if $b_k\le\delta$ almost surely for every
$1\le k\le\kappa$, then, for the averages $\overline Z_j :=\frac1w\sum_{k=(j-1)w+1}^{jw}Z_k$ on deterministic bins, we have, for every $H>\delta$,
\[
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \max_{1\le j\le\lfloor\kappa/w\rfloor}
        \overline Z_j>H
    \right)
    \le
    \left\lfloor\frac{\kappa}{w}\right\rfloor
    \exp\left\{-\frac{w(H-\delta)^2}{6}\right\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Concentration of bin averages

label: eq:bin_conditional_mgf
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $X_k:=Z_k-b_k$. Conditionally on $\mathcal{F}_k$, the variable $X_k$ has mean zero and is supported on an interval of length at most $2\sqrt3$. Conditional Hoeffding's inequality therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X_k}\mid\mathcal{F}_k]
 \ \le \  e^{3\lambda^2/2},
 \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
For every deterministic starting index $s$, successive conditioning
on $\mathcal{F}_{s+w-1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_s$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bin_conditional_mgf}
    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \exp\left\{\lambda\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{s+r}\right\}
        \,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_s
    \right]
    \le e^{3w\lambda^2/2}.
\end{equation}

To handle the random starting index $S$, observe that
$\{S=s\}\in\mathcal{F}_s$ because $S$ is a stopping time. Thus,
using~\eqref{eq:bin_conditional_mgf},
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \exp\left\{\lambda\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r}\right\}
    \right]
    &=
    \sum_{s=1}^{\kappa-w+1}
    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \mathbf1_{\{S=s\}}
        \exp\left\{\lambda\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{s+r}\right\}
    \right]
    \\
    &=
    \sum_{s=1}^{\kappa-w+1}
    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \mathbf1_{\{S=s\}}
        \mathbb{E}\left[
            \exp\left\{\lambda\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{s+r}\right\}
            \,\middle|\,\mathcal{F}_s
        \right]
    \right]
    \\
    &\le
    e^{3w\lambda^2/2}
    \sum_{s=1}^{\kappa-w+1}\mathbb{P}(S=s)
    =
    e^{3w\lambda^2/2}.
\end{align*}
Chernoff's bound, with $\lambda=t/3$ for the upper tail and $\lambda=-t/3$ for the lower tail, gives, for every $t>0$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left(\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r}\ge t\right)
 \ \le \  e^{-wt^2/6}
  \quad \text{ and } \quad
 \mathbb{P}\left(\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r}\le-t\right)
 \ \le \  e^{-wt^2/6}.
\end{align*}

Under the assumption of (i), on $\mathcal E$,
\[
    \overline Z_S
    \le \delta+\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r}.
\]
Consequently, $\mathcal E\cap\{\overline Z_S>H\}$ implies
$\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r}>H-\delta$, proving (i).
Similarly, under the assumption of (ii), on $\mathcal E$,
\[
    \overline Z_S
    \ge z+\frac1w\sum_{r=0}^{w-1}X_{S+r},
\]
and the lower-tail bound proves (ii).
Finally, the assertion for deterministic bins follows from (i)
with $\mathcal E=\Omega$ and a union bound.

label: lemma:FN_bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:FN_bound}
Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge1}\) be a filtration, and let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_w\) be random variables such that \(Z_k\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{k+1}\)-measurable. 
Assume that $Z_k\in[-\sqrt 3,\sqrt 3]$ almost surely and that \( \min_{1 \le k \le w} \mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal F_{k}]\ge z .\) 
Then, for every \(H<z\), 
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \frac1w\sum_{k=1}^w Z_k \le H \right)
 \ \le \  \exp\left\{ -\frac{w(z-H)^2}{6} \right\}. 
\]
head: environment
name: False-negative bound

title: Proof
body_md:
Set \( X_k:=Z_k-\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}].\)
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:FP_bound}, the variables \(X_k\) form a bounded martingale-difference sequence and satisfy the conditional Hoeffding bound
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \sum_{k=1}^w X_k<-wt \right)
 \ \le \  \exp\left(-\frac{w t^2}{6}\right).
\]
Because \(\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal F_{k}]\ge z\), we have
$\sum_{k=1}^w Z_k \ \ge \  \sum_{k=1}^w X_k+wz .$ 
Therefore,
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \frac1w\sum_{k=1}^w Z_k \le H \right)
 \ \le \  \mathbb{P}\left( \sum_{k=1}^w X_k\le -w(z-H) \right)
 \ \le \  \exp\left\{ -\frac{w(z-H)^2}{6} \right\}.
\]

label: eq:EZ_exact
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $d_n:=np_n$ and $m_k:=p_nk(n-k)$.
Whenever $C_k>0$, the conditional law
$a_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k\sim\operatorname{Exp}(C_k)$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:EZ_exact}
    \mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]
    =\sqrt3\,\frac{C_k-m_k}{C_k+m_k}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:first-entry}, the event $H:=\{K_1\le n^{1-\alpha}\log n\}$ has probability $1-o(1)$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{(i) Pre-change.}
Couple the planted graph with
$\widetilde G\sim G(n,p_n)$ so that they agree on every pair
outside $\binom{V_1}{2}$, and use the same source and transmission
weights on shared edges.
Before the first visit to $V_1$, no internal edge of $V_1$ can
affect the exploration. Thus the two explorations and their cut
sizes coincide for every $k<K_1$.

On $H$, we have $K_1<n/2$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:homogeneous-cut-concentration}, applied to
$\widetilde G$, therefore gives, with high probability,
\[
    \sup_{1\le k<K_1}
    \left|\frac{C_k}{m_k}-1\right|
    \le\delta_n
    \quad \text{ where } \quad 
    \delta_n:=\sqrt{\frac{24\log(ed_n)}{d_n}}=o(1).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:EZ_exact}, we obtain on this event
$\sup\limits_{1\le k<K_1} \bigl|\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]\bigr|
 \le\frac{\sqrt3\,\delta_n}{2-\delta_n}
 = o(1),
$
which proves (i).

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{(ii) Post-change.}
Fix $D>0$ and consider $K_1\le k\le K_1+D\log n$.
Because $d_n\log n=o(n_1)$, we may apply Proposition~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd}(i) with $m_n=\lceil D\log n\rceil+1=o(n_1/d_n)$.
Together with $\mathbb{P}(H)=1-o(1)$, this gives, with high probability, $I_1(k)=j$ (where $j:=k-K_1+1$) uniformly over the stated interval. 
Thus,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Dk_early_dense}
    D_k:=I_1(k)(n_1-I_1(k))
    =j(n_1-j)\ge\frac12jn_1
\end{equation}
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Proposition~\ref{prop:G_npbx_cut_bound} gives
$C_k\ge\xi D_k-\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}$ with high probability.
Uniformly over the interval,
\[
 \frac{\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}}{D_k}
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n_1}}\right) \ = \  o(1),
\]
with $\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}=0$ when $\xi=1$.
As $\xi>0$ is fixed, \eqref{eq:Dk_early_dense} therefore yields
\begin{equation*}
                                
    C_k\ge cjn_1
\end{equation*}
for some constant $c>0$, uniformly with high probability.

Using $k=K_1+j-1$ and $j\ge1$, we obtain on $H$
\begin{align*}
 \frac{m_k}{C_k}
 \ \le \  C\frac{d_n(K_1+j)}{jn_1} 
 \ \le \  C\left( \frac{d_n n^{1-\alpha}\log n}{n_1} + \frac{d_n}{n_1} \right)
 \ = \  o(1),
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows from
$d_n\log n=o(n^{2\alpha-1})$ and $n_1\asymp n^\alpha$.
All these bounds are uniform over the stated interval.
Finally, \eqref{eq:EZ_exact} gives
\[
 \left|\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]-\sqrt3\right|
 \ = \  \frac{2\sqrt3\,m_k}{C_k+m_k}
 \ \le \  2\sqrt3\,\frac{m_k}{C_k}.
\]
Hence $\max\limits_{K_1\le k\le K_1+D\log n} \left|\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]-\sqrt3\right|
 \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$, which proves (ii).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first work with the oracle variables $Z_k$. 
By Lemma~\ref{lem:PIT_plugin_stability} and Corollary~\ref{cor:p_hat_rate}, $\sup_{k\le n/2}|\widehat Z_k-Z_k|=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$. Hence it is enough to establish the result for the oracle bin averages, and to transfer the conclusion to the feasible averages, we will introduce a fixed margin $\eta>0$ around the threshold $H_1=z/2$.


If necessary, set $Z_k=0$ once the cut vanishes; with probability $1-o(1)$, this convention is never used in the observation window.
Moreover, we write $b_k:=\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]$. 
Because $c>12/z^2$ and $H_1=z/2$, we may choose fixed $\eta,\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:K1_eta_choice}
    H_1+\eta<z,
    \qquad
    H_1-\eta-\epsilon>0,
    \qquad
    \frac{c(H_1-\eta-\epsilon)^2}{6}>\frac12.
\end{equation}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:first-entry}, because $\alpha>1/2$ and $\kappa_1=\Theta(\sqrt n)$, we have  $\mathbb{P}(K_1\le\kappa_1-2w)=1-o(1).$
Together with Lemma~\ref{lm:jump_size},
Lemma~\ref{lem:PIT_plugin_stability}, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:p_hat_rate}, this gives an event
$\mathcal E_n$, with $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_n)=1-o(1)$, on which
\begin{align*}
 K_1\le\kappa_1-2w,
 \quad
 \sup_{k<K_1}b_k\le\epsilon,
 \quad 
 \inf_{K_1\le k\le K_1+2w}b_k\ge z, 
 \quad
 \sup_{k\le n/2}|\widehat Z_k-Z_k|\le\eta.
\end{align*}
For the post-entry drift bound, we apply
Lemma~\ref{lm:jump_size}(ii) with any fixed $D>2c$.

Let $B_j:=\{(j-1)w+1,\ldots,jw\}$, $L_1:=\lfloor\kappa_1/w\rfloor$, and $j_1:=\lceil K_1/w\rceil.$
On $\mathcal E_n$, the bin $B_{j_1+1}$ is entirely contained in the search window, and the oracle and feasible bin averages $Z_j$ and $\hat{Z}_j$ differ by at most $\eta$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{No crossing before $K_1$.}
For each deterministic bin $B_j$, define $\mathcal E_{n,j}:=\mathcal E_n\cap\{jw<K_1\}.$ 
On this event, $b_k\le\epsilon$ throughout $B_j$.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:FP_bound}(i), applied with starting index $(j-1)w+1$ and threshold $H_1-\eta$, therefore gives
\[
 \mathbb{P}\bigl( \mathcal{E}_{n,j}\cap \{\overline Z_j>H_1-\eta\} \bigr)
 \ \le \  \exp\left\{-\frac{w(H_1-\eta-\epsilon)^2}{6}\right\}.
\]
Because $j<j_1$ is equivalent to $jw<K_1$, a union bound yields
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left( \mathcal{E}_n\cap \{\exists j<j_1:\overline Z_j>H_1-\eta\} \right) 
 \ \le \  L_1\exp\left\{ - \frac{w(H_1-\eta-\epsilon)^2}{6} \right\}
 \ = \  o(1),
\end{align*}
by~\eqref{eq:K1_eta_choice} and $L_1=O(\sqrt n/\log n)$.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{Crossing immediately after $K_1$.}
Round $K_1$ up to the next bin start and cap the result at
$\kappa_1$, defining the bounded stopping time
\[
    S:=\min\{w\lceil K_1/w\rceil+1,\kappa_1\}.
\]
For sufficiently large $n$, we have
$S+w-1\le\kappa_1+w-1\le n/2$.
On $\mathcal E_n$, the cap is inactive and
$\{S,\ldots,S+w-1\}=B_{j_1+1}$.
This bin lies entirely between $K_1$ and $K_1+2w$, so
$b_k\ge z$ throughout it.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:FP_bound}(ii), with event $\mathcal E_n$
and threshold $H_1+\eta$, gives
\[
 \mathbb{P}\left( \mathcal{E}_n\cap \{\overline Z_{j_1+1}\le H_1+\eta\} \right)
 \ \le \  \exp\left\{-\frac{w(z-H_1-\eta)^2}{6}\right\}
 \ = \  o(1).
\]

Combining these bounds with $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_n^c)=o(1)$, we find that, with probability $1-o(1)$, no feasible bin strictly preceding $B_{j_1}$ crosses $H_1$, whereas $B_{j_1+1}$ does.
The first crossing therefore occurs in $B_{j_1}$ or $B_{j_1+1}$.
Because the algorithm returns $(j-1)w$ for the first crossing bin, and $(j_1-1)w<K_1\le j_1w$, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\bigl(|\widehat K_1-K_1|\le w\bigr) \ = \  1-o(1).
\end{align*}

label: eq:EZ_C_over_m
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall from the proof of Lemma~\ref{lm:jump_size} that 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:EZ_C_over_m}
    \mathbb E[Z_k\mid \mathcal F_k]
    =
    \sqrt 3\,
    \frac{C_k-m_k}{C_k+m_k}, 
\end{equation}
where $m_k:=p_nk(n-k)$.
Thus, for part~(i) it is enough to prove that $m_k/C_k=o(1)$
uniformly over the stated range, while for part~(ii) it is enough to
prove that $C_k/m_k=1+o(1)$ uniformly.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{Proof of (i).}
Write $j:=k-K_1+1$ and $R_k:=n_1-I_1(k)$. 
By Lemma~\ref{lem:first-entry}, with high probability $K_1\le n^{1-\alpha}\log n=o(s_n).$ 
Moreover, Proposition~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd} gives, uniformly over the
range considered,
\[
 j-Cnp_n\log n \ \le \  I_1(k)\ \le \  j.
\]
Because $j\ge s_n-b\log n$ and $np_n\log n=o(s_n)$, it follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:I1_comparable_j}
    I_1(k)=(1-o(1))j
    \quad \text{ and } \quad 
    k=(1+o(1))j,
\end{equation}
uniformly for $K_1+s_n-b\log n \le k \le K_2^{\star} - r_n$.

At the other endpoint, $k\le K_2^\star-r_n=K_1+n_1-r_n$, and hence, using the deterministic bound $I_1(k)\le k-K_1+1$,
\[
 R_k = n_1-I_1(k)
 \ \ge \  n_1-(k-K_1+1)
 \ \ge \  r_n-1
 \ = \  (1-o(1))r_n.
\]

Set $D_k:=I_1(k)R_k$ and $M_k:=\min\{I_1(k),R_k\}$. 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:G_npbx_cut_bound}, with high probability, uniformly over $k$, we have 
\[
    C_k\ \ge \  \xi D_k-\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}.
\]
If $\xi<1$, then
\[
    \frac{\Delta_k^{\mathrm{in}}}{D_k}
    \le
    C
    \sqrt{
        \frac{M_k\log(en_1)}{D_k}
    }
    =
    C
    \sqrt{
        \frac{\log(en_1)}
             {\max\{I_1(k),R_k\}}
    }
    \le
    C
    \sqrt{\frac{2\log(en_1)}{n_1}}
    =
    o(1),
\]
while for $\xi=1$ the fluctuation term is zero. Hence, uniformly over
the range considered,
\[
    C_k\ \ge \  c\,I_1(k)R_k
\]
for some constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$.

Using \eqref{eq:I1_comparable_j}, we therefore obtain
\[
 \frac{m_k}{C_k}
 \ \le \  C\frac{p_nkn}{I_1(k)R_k}
 \ \le \  C'\frac{np_n}{R_k}
 \ \le \  C''\frac{np_n}{r_n}
 \ = \  o(1),
\]
uniformly for \(K_1+s_n-b\log n\le k\le K_2^\star-r_n\). 
Equation~\eqref{eq:EZ_C_over_m} then gives
\[
    \mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal F_k]
    =
    \sqrt3(1-o(1)).
\]

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{Proof of (ii).}
Fix $B>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:post_dense_cut}~(i),
\[
    \varepsilon_n
    :=
    \sup_{
        K_2\le k\le
        K_2+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil
    }
    \left|
        \frac{C_k}{p_nk(n-k)}-1
    \right|
    =
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]
Hence, with probability tending to one, $\varepsilon_n=o(1)$ and,
uniformly over the same interval,
\[
    \left|\frac{C_k}{m_k}-1\right|
    \le \varepsilon_n.
\]
On the event $\{\varepsilon_n<1\}$, Equation~\eqref{eq:EZ_C_over_m}
therefore yields
\[
    \left|
        \mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal F_k]
    \right|
    =
    \sqrt3
    \left|
        \frac{C_k/m_k-1}{C_k/m_k+1}
    \right|
    \le
    \sqrt3\,
    \frac{\varepsilon_n}{2-\varepsilon_n}
    =
    o(1)
\]
uniformly for $K_2 \le k\le K_2+\lceil Bnp_n\log n\rceil.$ 
This proves the second claim.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $d_n:=np_n$, $b_k:=\mathbb{E}[Z_k\mid\mathcal{F}_k]$, and set $r_n:=d_n\log n$ and $s_n^\circ:=\frac12\bigl(\sqrt n+d_n\log^2 n\bigr).$ 
As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:K1_detection},
extend $Z_k$ by zero after extinction if necessary.
Our assumptions imply
\[
    n^{1-\alpha}\log n+d_n\log n
    \ll s_n^\circ\ll n_1,
    \qquad
    d_n\ll r_n\ll n_1,
    \qquad
    w=o(r_n).
\]
Thus Lemma~\ref{lm:K_2_Z_exp} applies with
$s_n=s_n^\circ$ and $r_n=d_n\log n$.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:p_hat_rate},
\[
    \widehat s_n
    =(1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1))\bigl(\sqrt n+d_n\log^2 n\bigr).
\]
Hence, $\widehat s_n-s_n^\circ\gg w$ with high probability, and $\widehat s_n=o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$.
The first bin inspected by the endpoint procedure has first index
\[
    q_n
    :=\widehat K_1
      +w\left\lceil\frac{\widehat s_n}{w}\right\rceil+1
    =K_1+\widehat s_n+\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(w),
\]
where we used Proposition~\ref{prop:K1_detection}.
It follows that, with high probability,
\[
    K_1+s_n^\circ \ \le \  q_n \ \le \  K_2,
\]
since $K_2\ge K_1+n_1$ whenever $V_1$ is fully explored.
Moreover, Lemma~\ref{lem:first-entry} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd} give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:K2_completion_error}
    0\le K_2-K_2^\star=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n),
    \qquad
    K_2+r_n=o_{\mathbb{P}}(n).
\end{equation}

Because
$\frac{c(z-H_2)^2}{6} = \frac{3cz^2}{32}>1,$ 
we may choose fixed $\eta,\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small such that 
$H_2+\eta<z$, $\epsilon+2\eta<H_2$, and $\frac{c(z-H_2-\eta)^2}{6}>1.$ 
Let $\kappa:=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ and
\[
    \mathcal{K}_n:=[K_1+s_n^\circ,\;K_2^\star-r_n].
\]
The preceding estimates, Lemma~\ref{lm:K_2_Z_exp}, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:PIT_plugin_stability} yield an event
$\mathcal E_n$, with $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_n)=1-o(1)$, on which
\begin{align*}
    K_1+s_n^\circ\le q_n\le K_2,
    \quad
    K_2+r_n\le\kappa,
    \quad 
    \inf_{k\in\mathcal{K}_n}b_k\ge z,
    \quad
    \sup_{K_2\le k\le K_2+r_n}b_k\le\epsilon,
    \quad
    \sup_{k\le\kappa}|\widehat Z_k-Z_k|\le\eta.
\end{align*}

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{(i) No stopping substantially before $K_2^\star$.}
For every deterministic bin
$B_j:=\{(j-1)w+1,\ldots,jw\}$, define
$\mathcal E_{n,j} :=\mathcal E_n\cap\{B_j\subseteq\mathcal{K}_n\}.$ 
On $\mathcal E_{n,j}$, the drift satisfies $b_k\ge z$ throughout $B_j$.
Lemma~\ref{lemma:FP_bound}(ii), with threshold $H_2+\eta$, therefore gives
\[
    \mathbb{P}\bigl(
        \mathcal E_{n,j}\cap
        \{\overline Z_j\le H_2+\eta\}
    \bigr)
    \le
    \exp\left\{-\frac{w(z-H_2-\eta)^2}{6}\right\}.
\]
Taking a union bound over all
$L:=\lfloor\kappa/w\rfloor$ deterministic bins yields
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{P}\left( \mathcal E_n\cap \{\exists j\le L: B_j\subseteq\mathcal{K}_n,\; \overline Z_j\le H_2+\eta\} \right)
 \ \le \  L\exp\left\{-\frac{w(z-H_2-\eta)^2}{6}\right\}
 \ = \  o(1).
\end{align*}
Here the last equality follows from $L=O(n/\log n)$
and the choice of $\eta$.

Outside this exceptional event, on $\mathcal E_n$,
every feasible bin average corresponding to a bin contained
in $\mathcal{K}_n$ exceeds $H_2$.
Since the first inspected bin starts at or after
$K_1+s_n^\circ$, any downward crossing must occur in a bin
whose last index exceeds $K_2^\star-r_n$.
The reported left endpoint therefore satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:K2_lower_localization}
    \widehat K_2\ge K_2^\star-r_n-w,
\end{equation}
whenever the procedure finds a crossing.

\smallskip
\noindent
\textit{(ii) Stopping shortly after completion of $V_1$.}
Consider the bounded stopping time
\[
    S:=\min\left\{
        w\left\lceil\frac{K_2}{w}\right\rceil+1,\;
        \kappa-w+1
    \right\}.
\]
On $\mathcal E_n$, for sufficiently large $n$, the cap is
inactive, since $2w\le r_n$ and $K_2+r_n\le\kappa$.
Thus $S$ is the first index of the bin
$B_\ell$, where $\ell:=\lceil K_2/w\rceil+1$.
This bin lies entirely in $[K_2,K_2+r_n]$, so its drift
is bounded above by $\epsilon$ on $\mathcal E_n$.

Lemma~\ref{lemma:FP_bound}(i), with threshold $H_2-2\eta$,
gives
\[
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \mathcal E_n\cap
        \{\overline Z_\ell>H_2-2\eta\}
    \right)
    \le
    \exp\left\{
        -\frac{w(H_2-2\eta-\epsilon)^2}{6}
    \right\}
    =o(1).
\]
On the complementary event within $\mathcal E_n$,
the feasible average in this bin is at most
$H_2-\eta<H_2$.
Furthermore, $q_n\le K_2$, so this bin is eligible for
the endpoint search.
The procedure therefore finds a crossing no later than
$B_\ell$, giving
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:K2_upper_actual}
    \widehat K_2
    \le(\ell-1)w
    \le K_2+w.
\end{equation}

Combining the two exceptional-probability bounds with
$\mathbb{P}(\mathcal E_n^c)=o(1)$, both
\eqref{eq:K2_lower_localization} and
\eqref{eq:K2_upper_actual} hold with high probability.
Together with~\eqref{eq:K2_completion_error} and
$w=o(r_n)$, they imply
\[
    |\widehat K_2-K_2^\star|
    =\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n)
    =\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np_n\log n).
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
We derive in this section the consistency rate for \(\widehat\alpha\) from the localization bounds for the dense-phase endpoints. Define $\widehat n_1:=\widehat K_2-\widehat K_1$ and $\widehat\alpha:=\frac{\log \widehat n_1}{\log n}$.
By the triangle inequality, 
\begin{align*}
|\widehat n_1-n_1|
\ = \  
\left|
(\widehat K_2-\widehat K_1)
-
(K_2^\star-K_1)
\right| 
\ \le \ 
|\widehat K_2-K_2^\star|
+
|\widehat K_1-K_1|.
\end{align*}
The bounds $|\widehat K_1-K_1|=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P}(\log n)$ and $|\widehat K_2-K_2^\star| =\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P}\!\left(pn\log n\right)$ together with $np \gg 1$ give  
\[
|\widehat n_1-n_1|
\ = \ 
\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb P}\!\left(pn\log n\right).
\]
Since \(n_1=\lfloor n^\alpha\rfloor\), this error is \(o_{\mathbb P}(n_1)\)
under the standing assumptions. Hence $\frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1} \ \to \  1$ in probability.

We now pass from \(\widehat n_1\) to \(\widehat\alpha\). 
Since $n_1=n^\alpha( 1 + \mathcal{O}(n^{-\alpha}) )$, we have $\log n_1=\alpha\log n+\mathcal{O}(n^{-\alpha})$. Therefore
\begin{align}
|\widehat\alpha-\alpha| 
\ = \  \left| \frac{\log \widehat n_1}{\log n} - \alpha \right| 
& \ \le \  \frac{1}{\log n} \left| \log\widehat n_1-\log n_1 \right| + \frac{1}{\log n} \left| \log n_1 - \alpha \log n \right| \nonumber \\ 
                                                                                                                          
& \ = \  \frac{1}{\log n} \left| \log\left(\frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1}\right) \right| + \mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac1{n^{\alpha} \log n}\right). \label{eq:in_proof_alpha}
\end{align}
Observe that the map \(x \in [1/2,3/2] \mapsto\log x\) is Lipschitz, since \(|(\log x)'|=1/x\le2\) on \([1/2,3/2]\). 
Since \(\widehat n_1/n_1\to1\) in probability, the event $\{ \frac12\le \frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1}\le \frac32 \}$ has probability tending to one. On this event, we have 
\[
    \left|
        \log\left(\frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1}\right)
    \right|
    \ \le \ 
    2\left|
        \frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1}-1
    \right|
    \ = \ 
    2\frac{|\widehat n_1-n_1|}{n_1}
\]
with probability tending to one. Hence
\[
    \log\left(\frac{\widehat n_1}{n_1}\right)
    =
    O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(
        \frac{|\widehat n_1-n_1|}{n_1}
    \right).
\]
Consequently, going back to Equation~\eqref{eq:in_proof_alpha} we obtain 
\[
\left| \widehat\alpha-\alpha \right| 
\ = \  O_{\mathbb P}\!\left(\frac{pn\log n}{n^\alpha\log n}\right) + O\!\left(\frac1{n^{\alpha} \log n}\right).
\]

body_md:
Set $Y_k:=p\,k(n-k)X_k$ and $S:=\frac1M\sum_{k\in\mathcal W}Y_k$, so that we have $ \frac{ \hat{p}_{{\rm MLE}\xspace} }{ p } =S^{-1}$.
The lemma's assumptions on the rates give
$\frac1{1+\varepsilon_+}
 \le \mathbb{E}[Y_k]
 \le \frac1{1-\varepsilon_-},$ 
and hence $|\mathbb{E}[S]-1|\le\varepsilon$.

Because $\mu_kX_k\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, there exists an absolute constant $C_0>0$ such that
\[
 \|Y_k-\mathbb{E}[Y_k]\|_{\psi_1} \ \le \  \frac{C_0}{1-\varepsilon_-}.
\]
By Bernstein's inequality for independent sub-exponential variables
\citep[Section~2.8]{vershynin2018high}, there exists an absolute
constant $C>0$ such that, for every $x\ge0$, with probability
at least $1-2e^{-x}$,
\[
 |S-\mathbb{E}[S]|
 \ \le \  \frac{C}{1-\varepsilon_-} \left(\sqrt{\frac{x}{M}}+\frac{x}{M}\right)
 \ = \  u(x).
\]
On this event, $|S-1|\le\varepsilon+u(x)$. If $\varepsilon+u(x)<1$, then $S\ge1-\varepsilon-u(x)>0$, and therefore
\[
 \frac{|\hat{p}_{{\rm MLE}\xspace}-p|}{p}
 \ = \  \left|\frac1S-1\right|
 \ = \  \frac{|S-1|}{S}
 \ \le \  \frac{\varepsilon+u(x)}{1-\varepsilon-u(x)}.
\]

body_md:
\label{lem:xi_window_approx}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:estimation}, we have 
$\widehat r_n
    =
    r_n^\circ+o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ),$ 
    $|\mathcal W_\xi\triangle\mathcal W_\xi^\circ| = o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ),$
and
$|\mathcal W_\xi|

name: Comparison of the feasible and oracle windows

title: Proof
body_md:
The localization bounds give $|\widehat K_1-K_1| = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(\log n)$ and $|\widehat K_2-K_2^\star| = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np\log n)$. Hence, 
$ |\widehat n_1-n_1| = \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np\log n+\log n).$ 
Moreover, by using $np\ll\frac{n^{2\alpha-1}}{\log n},$ 
$n_1\asymp n^\alpha,$ and $r_n^\circ\asymp\frac{n_1}{\log n},$ 
we obtain $np\log n=o(r_n^\circ)$ and $\log n=o(r_n^\circ).$
Therefore 
\[
    \widehat n_1
    =
    n_1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)
    \quad \text{ and } \quad 
    \widehat r_n
    =
    r_n^\circ+o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ).
\]

The left endpoints of the intervals $\mathcal W_\xi$ and
$\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$ differ by
\[
    (\widehat K_1-K_1)
    +
    (\widehat r_n-r_n^\circ)
    =
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ),
\]
and the same holds for the right endpoints. As the symmetric difference of two intervals is bounded by the sum of the difference of their endpoints, we obtain 
\[
    |\mathcal W_\xi\triangle\mathcal W_\xi^\circ|
    =
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ).
\]

Moreover,
$|\mathcal W_\xi^\circ|
    =
    n_1-2r_n^\circ+1
    =
    (1+o(1))n_1,$ 
because $r_n^\circ=o(n_1)$. Because 
\[
    \bigl|
        |\mathcal W_\xi|-|\mathcal W_\xi^\circ|
    \bigr|
    \ \le \ 
    |\mathcal W_\xi\triangle\mathcal W_\xi^\circ|
    \ = \  
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)
    \ = \  
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1),
\]
it follows that
\[
    |\mathcal W_\xi|
    =
    (1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1))n_1.
\]

Finally, $\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$ lies inside
$\mathcal W_\xi^+$ with a margin $r_n^\circ/2$ at each endpoint.
Since the corresponding endpoints of $\mathcal W_\xi$ differ from
those of $\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$ by $o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)$,
\[
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \mathcal W_\xi\cup\mathcal W_\xi^\circ
        \subseteq\mathcal W_\xi^+
    \right)
    \ = \  1-o(1).
\]

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:xi_bulk_approx}
Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:estimation},
uniformly for $k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+$,
\[
    \frac{\widehat B_k}{B_k}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),
    \qquad
    \frac{\widehat D_k}{D_k}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),
    \qquad 
    \frac{B_k}{q_0D_k}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),
    \qquad
    \frac{C_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]
head: environment
name: Uniform approximation on the bulk

title: Proof
body_md:
By Corollary~\ref{cor:p_hat_rate}, $\widehat p/p=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$, which immediately gives
$\frac{\widehat B_k}{B_k}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$. 
Uniformly on $\mathcal W_\xi^+$, Proposition~\ref{prop:I1_in_V1_bd} gives
\[
    I_1(k)
    =
    k-K_1+1+\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(np\log n).
\]
Because the buffer window remains at distance of order $r_n^\circ$ from both endpoints and $np\log n=o(r_n^\circ)$, we have $I_1(k)\ge c r_n^\circ$ and $n_1-I_1(k)\ge c r_n^\circ$ uniformly for some $c>0$. Together with Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_window_approx}, this implies
\[
 \widehat s_k = I_1(k)+o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)
 \quad \text{ and } \quad 
 \widehat n_1-\widehat s_k = n_1-I_1(k)+o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)
\]
uniformly on $\mathcal{W}_\xi^+$, and hence
$\sup_{ k \in \mathcal{W}_\xi^+ }\left| \frac{\widehat D_k}{D_k} - 1 \right| = o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$. 

Moreover,
$D_k = I_1(k)(n_1-I_1(k)) \ge c r_n^\circ n_1$
uniformly on $\mathcal W_\xi^+$. Because throughout the dense phase
$k=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(n^\alpha)$ and $n-k\asymp n$, we have 
$B_k=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(pn^{1+\alpha}),$ 
so
\[
    \sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}
    \frac{B_k}{q_0D_k}
    \ = \  
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}\left(\frac{np}{r_n^\circ}\right)
    \ = \  
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]

Finally, Proposition~\ref{prop:G_npbx_cut_bound} gives, uniformly on
$\mathcal W_\xi^+$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:in_proof_upper_bound_Ckbulk}
    |C_k-\mu_k(q_0)|
    \le
    \Delta_k^{\rm in}
    + U_k
    + p_n\bigl(k(n-k)-D_k\bigr).
\end{equation}
Since $\mu_k(q_0)=B_k+q_0D_k\ge q_0D_k$, it is enough to divide the
right-hand side by $q_0D_k$. Using the bounds established above,
$D_k\ge c r_n^\circ n_1$, $M_k\le n_1$, $n-k\asymp n$, and the fact
that $q_0=\xi-p_n$ is bounded away from zero, we obtain uniformly on
$\mathcal W_\xi^+$,
\[
 \frac{\Delta_k^{\rm in}}{q_0D_k}=o(1),
 \quad
 \frac{U_k}{q_0D_k}=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1),
 \quad \text{ and } \quad 
 \frac{p_n(k(n-k)-D_k)}{q_0D_k} \ \le \  \frac{B_k}{q_0D_k} \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]
We conclude that
$\sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+} \left| \frac{C_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}-1 \right| = o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).$

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $S_n^\circ(q_0)=A_n^\circ+M_n^\circ,$
where
$A_n^\circ := \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^\circ} D_k \left( \frac{1}{\mu_k(q_0)}-\frac{1}{C_k} \right)$ 
and
$M_n^\circ := \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^\circ} D_k \left( \frac{1}{C_k}-a_k \right).$

We first control the term $A_n^\circ$, caused by replacing the true rate $C_k$ by $\mu_k(q_0)$. 
By Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_bulk_approx}, uniformly on $\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$,
$\frac{C_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).$ 
Moreover,
\[
    \frac{D_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}
    \ \le \  \frac{1}{q_0}
    \ = \  \mathcal{O}(1),
\]
because $q_0=\xi-p\to\xi>0$. 
Hence
\begin{align}
\label{eq:in_proof_term_An}
 |A_n^\circ|
 \ \le \  |\mathcal W_\xi^\circ| \sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^\circ} \frac{D_k}{\mu_k(q_0)} \sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^\circ} \frac{|C_k-\mu_k(q_0)|}{C_k} 
 \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1).
\end{align}

We next control the random fluctuations.  Conditionally on $\mathcal J$, $\mathbb{E}[M_n^\circ\mid\mathcal J]=0$ 
and, by conditional independence,
\[
    \operatorname{Var}(M_n^\circ\mid\mathcal J)
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^\circ}
    \frac{D_k^2}{C_k^2}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_bulk_approx}, $\mu_k(q_0) = q_0D_k(1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)),$ uniformly on $\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$, 
because $B_k/(q_0D_k)=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$. 
Together with $C_k/\mu_k(q_0)=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$, this gives $C_k=q_0D_k(1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1))$ uniformly, and thus 
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(M_n^\circ\mid\mathcal J)
 \ = \  \frac{|\mathcal W_\xi^\circ|}{q_0^2} (1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1))
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1).
\]
Conditional Chebyshev's inequality then yields
\begin{align}
 \label{eq:in_proof_term_Mn}
 M_n^\circ
 \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(\sqrt{n_1})
 \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1).
\end{align}
We finish the proof by combining~\eqref{eq:in_proof_term_An} and~\eqref{eq:in_proof_term_Mn}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the feasible approximate log-likelihood is
\[
    \widehat\ell_n(q)
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi}
    \left(
        \log\widehat\mu_k(q)
        -
        a_k\widehat\mu_k(q)
    \right),
\]
and write its derivative as
\[
    \widehat S_n(q)
    :=
    \widehat\ell_n'(q)
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi}
    \widehat D_k
    \left(
        \frac{1}{\widehat\mu_k(q)}-a_k
    \right).
\]

\paragraph*{Step 1: Transfer the oracle bound to the feasible likelihood}
We first show that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:xi_score_small}
    \widehat S_n(q_0)=o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1).
\end{equation}
On the common part
$\mathcal W_\xi\cap\mathcal W_\xi^\circ$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_bulk_approx} gives $\frac{\widehat D_k}{D_k}=1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$ and $\frac{\widehat\mu_k(q_0)}{\mu_k(q_0)} =1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$, uniformly in $k$. Thus, 
$\frac{\widehat D_k}{\widehat\mu_k(q_0)} - \frac{D_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}
 = o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
$
Therefore the difference between the feasible and oracle scores on the
common part is bounded by
\begin{align*}
&|\mathcal W_\xi|
\sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}
\left|
    \frac{\widehat D_k}{\widehat\mu_k(q_0)}
    -
    \frac{D_k}{\mu_k(q_0)}
\right| 
+
\sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+} \left| \frac{\widehat D_k}{D_k}-1 \right|
\sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}a_kD_k .
\end{align*}
The first term is $o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$.  For the second, conditionally on
$\mathcal J$,
\[
    \mathbb{E}\left[
        \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}a_kD_k
        \,\middle|\,
        \mathcal J
    \right]
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}\frac{D_k}{C_k}
    =
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1),
\]
and its conditional variance is also $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$.
Thus
\[
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}a_kD_k
    =
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1),
\]
and the contribution from the common part is $o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$.

It remains to control the indices that belong to only one of the two
windows.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_window_approx},
$|\mathcal W_\xi\triangle\mathcal W_\xi^\circ| = o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ),$
and, with probability tending to one, all these indices belong to
$\mathcal W_\xi^+$.  Moreover, Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_bulk_approx} implies
uniformly on $\mathcal W_\xi^+$ that
\[
    \max\left\{ 
    \frac{D_k}{C_k},
    \frac{\widehat D_k}{C_k},
    \frac{D_k}{\mu_k(q_0)},
    \frac{\widehat D_k}{\widehat\mu_k(q_0)}
    \right\}
    \ = \  \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]
Conditionally on $\mathcal J$, the variables
$\{C_ka_k:k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+\}$ are independent $\operatorname{Exp}(1)$, so
$\max_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi^+}C_ka_k
    =
    \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(\log n).
$ 
Hence each score contribution on the symmetric difference is $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(\log n)$ uniformly, and their total contribution is $o_{\mathbb{P}}(r_n^\circ)\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}(\log n) = o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$,
because $r_n^\circ\log n=(1+o(1))n_1$.
Together with Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_oracle_score}, this proves
\eqref{eq:xi_score_small}.

\paragraph*{Step 2: Control the curvature of the likelihood}
We have
\[
    -\widehat\ell_n''(q)
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi}
    \frac{\widehat D_k^2}{\widehat\mu_k(q)^2}
    =
    \sum_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi}
    \frac{1}{
        \left(q+\widehat B_k/\widehat D_k\right)^2
    }.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:xi_bulk_approx},
$\sup_{k\in\mathcal W_\xi}
    \frac{\widehat B_k}{\widehat D_k}
    =
    o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).$
Because $q_0\to\xi>0$ and
$|\mathcal W_\xi|=(1+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1))n_1$, for every sufficiently small fixed
$\varepsilon>0$ there exists $c_\varepsilon>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:xi_curvature}
    \mathbb{P}\left(
        \inf_{|q-q_0|\le\varepsilon}
        \bigl\{-\widehat\ell_n''(q)\bigr\}
        \ge c_\varepsilon n_1
    \right)
    \longrightarrow1.
\end{equation}
Thus moving $q$ a fixed distance away from $q_0$ changes the derivative
of the likelihood by an amount of order $n_1$, whereas
\eqref{eq:xi_score_small} shows that the derivative at $q_0$ is
$o_{\mathbb{P}}(n_1)$.

\paragraph*{Step 3: Localize the maximizer.}
Suppose first that $\xi<1$.  Fix $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that,
with probability tending to one,
$q_0-\varepsilon$ and $q_0+\varepsilon$ both belong to
$[0,1-\widehat p]$.  Since
$\widehat S_n'(q)=\widehat\ell_n''(q)$,
\eqref{eq:xi_score_small} and \eqref{eq:xi_curvature} imply
\begin{align}
    \widehat S_n(q_0-\varepsilon)>0
    \quad \text{ and } \quad 
    \widehat S_n(q_0+\varepsilon)<0,
 \label{eq:in_proof_score}
\end{align}
with probability tending to one. 
As $\widehat\ell_n$ is concave, its score $\widehat S_n$ is nonincreasing. Hence, the inequalities in ~\eqref{eq:in_proof_score} imply that every maximizer lies in $[q_0-\varepsilon,q_0+\varepsilon]$.

If $\xi=1$, the same argument at $q_0-\varepsilon$ gives $\widehat q\ge q_0-\varepsilon$ with probability tending to one. On the other hand, by the parameter constraint,
\[
 \widehat q
 \ \le \  1-\widehat p
 \ = \  q_0+(p-\widehat p)
 \ = \  q_0+o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).
\]
Thus, in both cases, $\widehat q-q_0=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1).$ 
Finally, because $\widehat p-p=o_{\mathbb{P}}(1)$, we conclude that 
\[
 \widehat\xi-\xi
 \ = \  (\widehat p-p)+(\widehat q-q_0)
 \ = \  o_{\mathbb{P}}(1). 
\]

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lm:algo_correctness}
 The cut size sequence $\left(C_k\right)_{k \in [n]}$ produced by \textsc{SampleCutSizes}$(n,p)$ has the same distribution as the sequence of cut sizes in a $G_{n,{p_n}}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the claim by coupling the algorithm with the FPP exploration of
\(G(n,p)\), using the deferred-decisions principle.

Let the FPP process start from a fixed vertex \(s\). For an infected set
\(\mathcal I_k\), define the cut-degree of an inactive vertex \(v\in \mathcal{I}_k^c\) by
$d_{\mathcal I_k}(v) = |\{u\in \mathcal I_k:(u,v)\in E\}|.$ 
The corresponding cut-degree histogram is $H_{\mathcal{I}_k}(i) = |\{v\in \mathcal{I}_k^c:d_{\mathcal I_k}(v)=i\}|$ and the cut size is $C_k=\sum_i iH_{\mathcal{I}_k}(i).$

We construct the graph exploration lazily. Initially, only the edges from the
source \(s\) to the other \(n-1\) vertices are revealed. Each such edge is
present independently with probability~\(p\). Therefore
$H_{\{s\}}(1)\sim \operatorname{Bin}(n-1,p),$ $H_{\{s\}}(0)=n-1-H_{\{s\}}(1),$ 
and \(H_{\{s\}}(i)=0\) for \(i\notin\{0,1\}\). This agrees with Line
\ref{ln:scs_init}.

Now suppose the current infected set is \(\mathcal I_k\), and write
$H(i)=H_{\mathcal I_k}(i).$ 
Let $C=\sum_i iH(i)$  be the current cut size. If \(C=0\), the connected component of the source has
been exhausted, and the cut size remains zero thereafter. Thus assume \(C>0\).

Conditionally on the currently revealed graph, the exponential clocks on the
cut edges are independent and have the same rate. By the memorylessness of the
exponential distribution, the next infection edge is therefore uniformly
distributed among the \(C\) cut edges. Hence, the probability that the newly
infected vertex has current cut-degree \(i\) is
\[
\frac{iH(i)}{\sum_j jH(j)}.
\]
This is exactly the sampling rule in Line \ref{ln:scs_sample_u}. After this
vertex is infected, it is removed from the inactive side, which corresponds to
subtracting one from the appropriate histogram bin, as in Line
\ref{ln:scs_rmv_u}.

It remains to update the cut-degrees of the remaining inactive vertices. Let
\(u\) be the newly infected vertex. For any remaining inactive vertex \(w\), the
edge \((u,w)\) was previously an edge between two inactive vertices. Hence it was
not revealed by the previous exploration. Since the underlying graph is
\(G(n,p)\), these edges are still conditionally independent Bernoulli\((p)\)
random variables.

Therefore, among the vertices that currently have cut-degree \(j\), the number
that are adjacent to \(u\) is distributed as $R_j\sim \operatorname{Bin}(H(j),p).$ 
Those \(R_j\) vertices move from bin \(j\) to bin \(j+1\). This is exactly the
promotion step in Lines \ref{ln:scs_sample_promotion}--\ref{ln:scs_calc_Ck}.
The descending order ensures that a vertex promoted from \(j\) to \(j+1\) is
not considered again in the same update.

Thus, the graph exploration and the algorithm can be coupled so that, at
every step, the histogram stored by the algorithm is exactly the cut-degree
histogram of the FPP exploration. Consequently, the cut size $C$ returned by the algorithm
has the same distribution as the cut size in the FPP exploration of \(G(n,p)\).
Therefore, the sequence returned by \textsc{SampleCutSizes} has the same
distribution as the true cut-size sequence.
